title: Governed Semantic Operation Language
description_html:
This paper introduces the Governed Semantic Operation Language, or GSOL, as a specification-layer language for representing computational operations as admissible semantic transitions before execution, lowering, or evidentiary use. GSOL is designed to make authority, effect, refusal, receipt, claim, nonclaim, standing, temporal validity, and lowering obligations explicit in a canonical operation form.

The paper positions GSOL as a constitutional interface between prose, policy, code, proof, and execution. It distinguishes capability from admissibility; testimony from evidence; evidence from authority; receipts from standing; and execution from semantic equivalence. GSOL is not proposed as a general-purpose programming language, runtime, truth engine, policy engine, or replacement for compiler intermediate representations. Instead, it is a governed semantic layer intended to preserve admissibility-relevant meaning across specification, implementation, verification, and lowering.

The paper defines GSOL's formal transition model, constitutional kernel, object model, claim and nonclaim discipline, refusal semantics, threat model, syntax sketch, worked model-invocation example, gap-certified lowering model, implementation feasibility, and limitations. It argues that governed computation needs a language of admissible operation: expressive enough to govern meaningful computational transitions, but deliberately not so computationally powerful that it becomes an opaque execution substrate.
